title: A shared pool of subscription accounts with CLIProxyAPI
text:
Problem 1 — one account for several people without a ban. The vendor blocks an account that works from several devices and IPs. Through the proxy, all requests come from one server under one authorization: to the vendor it is one client, while any number of people sit behind it, each with their own API key.

In practice. The chance of a block is substantially lower than with one account on different devices, but not zero: in six months, 2 of the 8 accounts in the pool were blocked. Keep that in mind.

Problem 2 — several accounts as one. Subscription limits burn fast. The pool is exposed to clients as one entry point, and the service itself moves requests to a fresh account when the current one runs out of quota.

The service accumulates OAuth authorizations of subscriptions (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Kimi, Grok) and API keys of providers such as OpenRouter, accepts requests over an OpenAI-compatible API and the native Anthropic and Gemini protocols, and serves one model list. Installation is in the README, details at help.router-for.me.

Security. All of the team's agent traffic — prompts, code, files, keys in context — goes through the proxy. Whoever gains access to it sees every request and can use the accounts. TLS only, a strong panel `secret-key`, a separate key per member, request-body `debug` logging off.

title: Pools for CLIProxyAPI: one model, every subscription
text:
CLIProxyAPI (CPA for short) is an open-source proxy from router-for-me. You run it on your own machine, sign in with the subscriptions you already have (Claude Code, ChatGPT Codex, Antigravity, Grok Build, Muse Code, Devin and others) or add API keys, and it serves all of them as one local API that speaks the OpenAI, Claude and Gemini formats.

That means any tool that can talk to an OpenAI- or Anthropic-style endpoint can use your subscriptions: Claude Code, Codex, the pi coding agent, your own scripts. You stop juggling a login per tool and a bill per vendor.

Your tools

- Claude Code
- Codex
- pi
- Your own scripts

→

CLIProxyAPI, on your machine

- One local API in the OpenAI, Claude and Gemini formats
- Spreads requests across your accounts
- Cools an account down at its limit

→

Your accounts

- Claude subscriptions
- Anthropic API keys
- ChatGPT Codex
- Devin
- OpenRouter

Your tools talk to one local endpoint. CPA sends each request to one of your accounts.

CPA also does the tedious parts of running several accounts. It spreads requests across them, can keep a conversation on the same account so its prompt cache stays warm, and puts an account on cooldown when it hits a limit and moves on to the next. It comes with a web console and supports plugins.

title: Pool Your Claude & Codex Subscriptions Behind a CLI Proxy (2026 Guide) — ModelDeck
text:
Some people don't want to pick an account at all — they want every subscription they own working as one pool. Instead of pointing Claude Code and Codex at their providers directly, you point them at a small proxy on your own machine. Every account is signed into that proxy, and it spreads requests across them, so a single long session draws from the whole pool instead of draining one plan. This guide sets that up end to end, then puts ModelDeck on top so you can see what the pool is actually doing.

The proxy used here is CLIProxyAPI — an open-source (MIT) proxy that exposes OpenAI-, Claude-, and Codex-compatible endpoints and handles the OAuth logins for you. It's a separate project, not part of ModelDeck; its docs live at help.router-for.me. What ModelDeck adds is the part a proxy can't show you: how much is actually left in each account it's routing to.

...

## 2 Sign each subscription into the pool

Run the login flag once per account — a browser opens, you sign in with that account, and the proxy writes a credential file for it into its auth directory. Repeat for every Claude and Codex subscription you own.

```
cli-proxy-api --claude-login   # OAuth callback on port 54545
cli-proxy-api --codex-login    # OAuth callback on port 1455
```

Add `--no-browser` to print the login URL instead of opening a window — useful over SSH.

title: Multi-Account Load Balancing | router-for-me/CLIProxyAPIDocs | DeepWiki
text:
This page describes CLIProxyAPI's multi-account load balancing system, which distributes requests across multiple accounts per AI provider using round-robin selection. This increases throughput, manages quota limits, and provides failover capabilities.

...

## Purpose and Scope Copy link to header

Multi-account load balancing allows CLIProxyAPI to:

- Distribute load: Spread requests across multiple accounts to avoid rate limits on any single account.
- Increase throughput: Utilize multiple accounts' quotas simultaneously.
- Provide failover: Automatically skip unavailable or disabled accounts.
- Manage quotas: Continue serving requests even when individual accounts reach their limits.

The system supports multi-account load balancing for all major providers, including Gemini, OpenAI Codex, Claude, Qwen, iFlow, Antigravity, and OpenAI-compatible providers.

## Account Selection Architecture Copy link to header

title: Explicit Account Routing in OpenCode with CLIProxyAPI
text:
I juggle between personal and work accounts for both Claude and Codex, and I wanted all of them available in OpenCode.

Most people set up local LLM proxies to pool their accounts into one bucket and auto-failover when a rate limit hits. I wanted the exact opposite. If I’m working on a company repo and hit a usage cap, the request should just fail. It should never quietly fall back to my personal account in the background.

I use CLIProxyAPI to handle the OAuth logins, token refreshes, and upstream requests. It supports account-specific prefixes, so I can give each login a clear label like `claude-work` or `codex-personal`.

...

In my OpenCode config, I pass the plugin the list of account prefixes I want exposed and whether each one speaks Anthropic or OpenAI under the hood:

```
{
  "accounts": [
    { "id": "claude-work", "provider": "anthropic" },
    { "id": "claude-personal", "provider": "anthropic" },
    { "id": "codex-work", "provider": "openai" },
    { "id": "codex-personal", "provider": "openai" }
  ]
}
```

...

Instead of storing a bearer token in `opencode.json`, the plugin fetches the local proxy key at runtime by shelling out to a small helper script (`~/.local/bin/cliproxyapi-key`). With that key, it polls `http://127.0.0.1:8317/v1/models` every 60 seconds to get the list of prefixed routes currently active in CLIProxyAPI (like `claude-work/claude-sonnet-5-5` or `codex-personal/gpt-6.1-sol`).

title: Account Pool | CodexUse
text:
Account Pool (Pro) lets Cursor, scripts, and other apps use your saved Codex accounts through one local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. When one account hits its limit, the next one takes over. It runs on your machine as a loopback endpoint, not a hosted proxy, so another app can reach all of those accounts through a single base URL and key.

 What it does: gives another app one base URL and one key while CodexUse shares quota across the selected accounts, load-balances fresh requests, and fails over before a response starts when another account is eligible.

...

## Native API engine

Account Pool uses the unmodified CLIProxyAPI engine to call the subscription-backed Codex backend over OAuth. It no longer converts API requests into app-server turns. The private engine binds to loopback with its own random key; client keys and account selection remain owned by CodexUse.

...

Not the billed OpenAI API: this uses the Codex subscription backend, not `api.openai.com`. Backend changes, account access, and upstream usage policies still apply. Compatibility does not make every OpenAI endpoint or parameter available.

## Set up the pool

1. Open CodexUse → Account Pool, or run `codexuse account-pool status`.
2. On the Accounts tab, select the accounts you want it to use, and choose a Pick order for new requests.
3. On the Overview tab, click Generate key and copy the key. CodexUse shows it only once.
4. Make sure Accept requests is on.

The base URL appears in the Connect an app section

title: CPA proxy deployment guide: CLIProxyAPI + NewAPI account-pool gateway | CCNavX
text:
In a CPA + NewAPI architecture, the roles are usually:

| Layer | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Account layer | Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, AI Studio, OpenAI-compatible upstreams |
| CPA layer | Turns accounts, OAuth sessions, or upstream keys into a unified API |
| NewAPI layer | Manages channels, users, tokens, quotas, model pricing, and the public endpoint |

...

A complete CPA proxy usually has two layers. CPA answers “how do accounts become an API?” NewAPI answers “how do I distribute that API to users?” If you only need private use, start with CPA alone. If multiple people need access, add a distribution layer.

title: heads/main/README_EN.md
text:
CLIProxyAPI Plus is a community enhanced build of CLIProxyAPI. It keeps the original project's broad provider compatibility and OpenAI-compatible gateway behavior, then adds a more operator-friendly Codex quota workflow:

- Codex quota cards show plan, balance, 5-hour usage, weekly usage, and reset windows.
- Auth-file cards show remaining quota directly under health status.
- Auth-file cards show total, cached, input, and output tokens plus API cost equivalent and estimated total capacity.
- Auth files can be sorted by Codex weekly quota remaining, high capacity first.
- Codex accounts can be automatically disabled after `usage_limit_reached`.
- Codex accounts can also be stopped early when weekly quota remaining is at or below a configurable threshold such as `3%` or `5%`.
- OAuth callback waiting is longer, which is friendlier for real browser login flows on remote servers.

...

Large account pools are tedious to operate manually. A single exhausted Codex credential can keep getting retried, burn refresh attempts, and hide the accounts that still have useful weekly capacity. CLIProxyAPI Plus makes the quota state visible and actionable:

- Use high-quota accounts first by sorting on weekly remaining quota.
- See how many tokens each account has actually carried, how much was cached, the API cost equivalent, and the estimated total capacity.
- Let low-quota accounts disable themselves before they hit the wall.
- Keep disabled accounts annotated with expected recovery time.

title: KarpelesLab/teamclaude: Multi-account proxy for Claude ...
text:
Multi-account proxy for Claude Code and Codex: it pools Claude Max, ChatGPT/Codex, API-key and third-party backend accounts, and rotates on quota.

It sits between the coding agent and the provider's API, holds several accounts, and moves to the next one when the current account gets close to its session or weekly limit. The session keeps running instead of stopping on a 429. Claude accounts serve Claude Code, Codex accounts serve the Codex CLI, and both pools share one proxy.

**It is built for one person.** The "team" is the agents: someone running ten, or fifty, coding-agent sessions at once needs more than one subscription, and switching accounts by hand each time one fills up is what this replaces. Every account in the pool is your own, and the client is the provider's own CLI. It is not a way to share an account between people, and not a bridge for other clients onto subscription credentials — see Scope.

...

- Rotates to the next account when the 5h session or 7d weekly bucket reaches the threshold (98% by default), preferring the account whose weekly quota resets soonest.
- Tracks the per-model weekly cap separately, so an account out of Fable quota is skipped for Fable requests and still serves Opus and Sonnet.
- Tells a spent quota bucket apart from a per-minute rate limit and only rotates on the first one. Rotating on a rate limit would just move the burst to the next account and drop the warm cache, so it paces the same account instead.

title: wjsoj/CPA-Claude
text:
- **Two endpoints, one fleet** — Claude on `:8317` (`/v1/messages`) and
 Codex on `:8318` (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`). Each can
 be enabled/disabled independently; the admin panel mounts on
 whichever is "primary" (Claude by default).
- **Native Claude passthrough** — no protocol translation for the
 Anthropic path, pure passthrough to
 `api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` (SSE streaming preserved).
- **Slot-based concurrency per OAuth file** — each OAuth credential has a
 `max_concurrent` cap. A client session that makes a request within the last
 10 minutes (configurable) occupies one slot. Idle clients release their
 slot automatically.
- **Per-credential upstream proxy** — every OAuth file may set its own
 `proxy_url`, useful when different accounts must egress from different IPs.
- **Persistent usage tracking** — input/output/cache-read/cache-write token
 counts per credential survive restarts in `state.json`.
- **API-key fallback** — when every OAuth credential is saturated, quota-
 exceeded, or dead, requests fall through to the unlimited API-key pool.
- **Codex API compatibility** — OpenAI-format `/v1/chat/completions` and
 `/v1/responses` on the Codex endpoint. API-key credentials forward to
 `api.openai.com`; OAuth (ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Team) credentials forward to

title: Turn AI CLI Subscriptions into OpenAI-Compatible APIs
text:
## Multi-Account Load Balancing

One of cliproxy's strongest features is multi-account load balancing. If you have two Claude Max accounts (or two Google accounts with Gemini access), you can authenticate both and cliproxy will round-robin requests between them.

To add a second account, run the login command again with a different account:

```bash
# First account
clipproxyapi --claude-login
# Log in with account-1@example.com

# Second account
clipproxyapi --claude-login
# Log in with account-2@example.com

```

Each login creates a separate token file in `~/.cli-proxy-api/`. The server detects new token files automatically and starts routing to the new account within seconds.

If one account hits a rate limit or returns an error, cliproxy automatically fails over to the next available account. When the failed account recovers, it rejoins the rotation.

...

- Token expiration silently breaks requests: OAuth tokens expire. Claude tokens last roughly a week, Gemini tokens refresh automatically but can fail if the refresh token is revoked. If you see 401 or "unauthorized" errors in cliproxy logs, re-authenticate. Set up a cron job or monitoring alert to catch expired tokens early.
- Port conflicts with other dev tools: The default port 8317 can conflict with other local services. If cliproxy fails to bind, check `lsof -i :8317` and either kill the conflicting process or change cliproxy's port in `config.yaml`.
